newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: CAUSLEY STILL WON'T RULE OUT LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE
Federal National Party MP Ian Causley says party leader Tim Fischer is still not addressing the needs of rural Australia.
Mr Causley says if no one else is prepared to stand up as a leadership candidate, he'll bring the issue forward.
The New South Wales MP says rural Australia is concerned about competition policy, the closure of services in rural areas and in particular, about the ramifications of the WIK decision.
Mr Causley says that at present, those concerns aren't being addressed.
CALL FOR COMAPNIES TO LOOK AT SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
The Federal Environment Minister says big business should face up to their social responsibilities, as well as its responsibilities to shareholders.
Robert Hill's concerns come following BHP's decision to close its steelmaking operation in Newcastle which will mean the shedding of thousands of jobs.
Senator Hill says it worries him that when BHP made the announcement, it was applauded in the financial press, and reacted to positively on the stock exchange.
He says while BHP's plan may be a sensible business decision, he'd like to see corporate Australia thinking about more than just the bottom line.
BEAZLEY WILL GIVE HIS SAVINGS REBATE TO CHARITY
Federal Opposition Leader Kim Beazley says he'll give his 450-dollar savings rebate to charity if he has to collect it.
Mr Beazley yesterday said he wouldn't claim the proposed 15-percent rebate because it should be means tested and available only to people on low incomes.
The Prime Minister's made the same pledge, but rejected calls to have the rebate means tested.
But Mr Beazley's told Radio 3AW in Melbourne, he's read newspaper reports suggesting Tax Office procedures won't allow him to refuse it, in which case he'll give it to charity.
MEDIA OWNERSHIP LAW CHANGES MAY BE DELAYED
Planned changes to media ownership laws may be delayed until later this year, with the Federal Government coming under mounting pressure not to rush the reforms.
Coalition MPs, concerned about a diminution of media diversity, are demanding to be consulted about any changes, and have already had two meetings with Communications Minister Richard Alston.
Senator Alston is considering reforms that include the scrapping of existing rules that prevent television station owners also controlling newspapers in the same market.
The Minister says he wants to consult as widely as possible and will hold further discussions with the Colaition's back-bench communications committee.
Government sources say Cabinet may not make a final decision now for up to six weeks, meaning any legislation won't be considered by Parliament until after its lengthy winter recess.
CHURCH ACCUSED OF FAILING TO ACCEPT RESPONSIBILITY FOR ABUSE
The Broken Rites group has accused the Catholic Church of failing to accept responsibility where its clergy sexually abuse parishioners.
The claim follows the conviction of Brother John Desmond Dyson on four counts of indecently assaulting young boys, while he was teaching at Victoria's Kilmore College in the 1980's.
Dyson later became Principal of the Catholic High School in Alice Springs.
Christine MacIsaac from the Broken Rites support group, says a senior church official was told about Dyson's behaviour in 1993, but did nothing.
NEW ROAD, CUSTOMS PROCEDURES, TERMINAL UPGRADES FOR SYDNEY
The Federal Transport Minister says a new report has convinced him that Sydney airport will be able to handle the demands of the year 2000 Olympic Games.
John Sharp has announced new measures designed to ensure the Airport will cope with increased passenger traffic during the Games.
Mr Sharp says there'll be no need to break flight curfews, or lift the cap of 80 flight movements per hour.
He says the report, from the Federal Transport Working Group, found there's sufficient runway and terminal capacity to deal with Olympic traffic.
The minister says however, that there'll be a new split level road build around the terminal, 300 milion dollars worth of terminal upgrades and improved customes procedures.
GOVT SAYS IT HAS NO CONTROL OVER ASHES BROADCASTING
The Federal Government says there's nothing it can do to force the Nine Network to show the first sessions of play of the upcoming cricket tests between Australia and England.
Nine has decided to stick with its normal prime-time programming and won't cross to the tests until 10.30 at night, to pick up play in the second and third sessions.
The office of Communications Minister, Richard Alston, says the Nine Network holds the free-to-air rights and it's up to them to decide how to use them.
ABC Television will screen the third cricket test from Old Trafford, because it co-incides with Nine's broadcast of the Wimbledon tennis finals.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
